recentItems.title: The Nepal mudslide: Disaster is not a traffic magnet
recentItems.description:
CGTN Host Nadim Diab explains how the Nepal mudslide has been distorted by a wave of misleading content, creating an alternative narrative that obscures the truth. He specifically debunks mislabeled old footage, misplaced glacier videos and AI-generated rescue clips, emphasizing that disasters must never be exploited to chase clicks at the expense of accuracy.#GoodPoint

recentItems.title: Ping-Pong at Songyue Lake: Shandong's carnival stop in Rizhao
recentItems.description:
At Songyue Lake in Wulian County, Rizhao City, ping-pong spent the weekend outdoors. The Shandong Ping-Pong Culture-Tourism Carnival put the national sport on the water and invited anyone to pick up a paddle.

Olympic champion Chen Meng was there. So were former China basketball player Gong Xiaobin, actor Feng Xiaotong, and the families who treated the shoreline in east China's Shandong Province as a court.

A few kilometers away, city teams were playing the Ping-Pong Super League at the sports center. Same county, two settings: a hall for the points, a lake for everyone else.

recentItems.title: With Merna: Finding common ground for the next generation
recentItems.description:
Earlier this year, Beijing's Temple of Heaven provided the setting for an important moment in China-US diplomacy. Beyond the headlines, the historic site is also part of everyday Beijing – a place where families gather and traditions are passed on.

There, CGTN Digital's Merna Al Nasser met Xiao Yi Jiejie (小一姐姐) and her daughter. Xiao Yi is a popular Chinese content creator with more than 20 million followers in China. What begins with a traditional Chinese finger dance opens into a conversation about family, culture and how traditions are passed on. Having also grown up across different cultures, Merna reflects on how, across cultures and societies, there is much we share and much we can learn from one another.

Perhaps common ground begins with something simple: the hopes we share for the next generation.

recentItems.title: What makes a good teacher?
recentItems.description:
Editor's note: September 10 marks China's Teachers' Day, a time to celebrate the teachers who shape and inspire generations. In this episode of Beyond ACG, we meet comic artist and educator Ruan Junting, who reflects on what it truly means to help students become themselves.

On her very first day as a teacher, Ruan Junting was caught off guard by a student's question: "If I don't want to become someone like you, do I still need to learn this?"

The question stayed with her for years, prompting her to reconsider what it means to teach, and what kind of person she wanted to be.

Ruan began drawing comics at 14 and has spent over two decades teaching art at the China Academy of Art. For years, she struggled between her artistic ambitions and the practical need to make a living. But her experiences with students gradually changed the way she understood art and education.

recentItems.title: Girl who lost family, adopted by teacher, aims to be educator too
recentItems.description:
September 10 is China's Teachers' Day, and a heartwarming story about a student and her teacher in southwest China's Sichuan Province is moving many people online.

When Zhang Zheng was eight, she had no relatives to rely on. The child lived alone in her family's modest tiled house. "I was always scared at night, so I kept a cleaver by my bed."

That was until her primary school teacher, Jiang Xianfang, asked her: "Would you like to come home with me?" That one question changed the girl's life.

From age 10 to 18, Zhang Zheng lived with Jiang's family. Two months after moving in, Zhang started calling her "mom."

This summer, Zhang scored 598 on the national college entrance examination, known as the gaokao, and was admitted to Sichuan Normal University as a government-funded student. She aims to return to her hometown to devote herself to education after graduation. She said: "I want to hold more children's hands, just as my teacher once held mine."

recentItems.title: Australian Harold Weldon: There's no end to the Long March
recentItems.description:
Harold Weldon from Australia been connected to #China for 40 years, ever since he retraced the #LongMarch as a teenager. A veteran sinologist, Weldon first walked the Red Army's historic route in 1985 at age 19, helping produce the landmark photographic book "China: The Long March." He retraced it again in 2011. From a village in northwest China's Sichuan Province to a nationwide high-speed rail network, he has witnessed the country's poverty alleviation and modernization first-hand."There's no end to the Long March,"  Weldon sighs with emotion. "It's the next horizon." #FrontlineStory

recentItems.title: Milo Yiannopoulos supported ICE, then he was deported
recentItems.description:
Far-right influencer Milo Yiannopoulos spent years calling for mass deportations. In 2025, he posted that the US must deport "millions and millions of people" and suggested ICE checkpoints at grocery stores and gas stations. Then, on August 27, 2026, ICE detained him at a Louisiana airport. He was deported to the UK the following day. DHS said he "chose to overstay his welcome in violation of our nation's laws" after legally entering in May 2019. Now, he says experiencing the system himself changed how he sees it. "I didn't really understand the physical reality how institutionalized the brutality is in America," he told Piers Morgan, describing the experience as "physically degrading," "disorientating" and "humiliating."

recentItems.title: Professor Brian Greene's AGI warning: 'Beyond human understanding'
recentItems.description:
Is AGI – human cognition-level Artificial General Intelligence – here? Depends who you ask – and what definition they're using. NVIDIA CEO Jensen Huang says "AGI has arrived" while Elon Musk predicts human-level AI is close. But researchers are divided, with some arguing the claim is corporate hype, not scientific fact. Theoretical physicist and Columbia University professor Brian Greene, who spoke with CGTN's Tian Wei, offers a different warning. He suggests AI may develop an intelligence radically different from our own – producing breakthroughs humans may not have the brain power to understand, and even finding the unified field theory, the holy grail of physics, that eluded Einstein. Are we ready for that future? #AGI #Podcast
